newsitem.title: UK: INSTANT VIEW - UK interest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - UK interest rate rise.

text.p: Following is a selection of economists' reactions to the rise in British interest rates. The Bank of England said it was raising official rates to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent.
"In line with expectations, should be well received by both sterling and Gilts."

"The quarter-point rise is the least that would have been required to keep the City (of London) happy. It has been on the cards for some time. He could have gone the whole hog and raised it by 50 basis points.
"Politically it would have been easier to get away with half a point and blame it on his predecessors, but this suggests he will have to raise rates again and fairly quickly."

"The pressure for an interest rate rise is no great surprise. My own feeling is the strength of sterling and weak industrial output means that inflation will be quite low. To raise interest rates without looking at fiscal policy is an interesting development."

"This was largely expected. The greater shock is from their decision to give the Bank of England independence in the setting of interest rates. That means we are close to a position where the UK is ready to join a single currency.

"My own view is that base rates should not be raised too aggressively before the year end. And I think that if (Gordon) Brown moves more towards fiscal policy to slow down growth, then the Bank of England will eventually see a less marked need for interest rate rises.

"A lot of people were talking about a 50-point rise. (The 25-point rise) has obviously got to be a good thing for the markets. It is seen as pre-emptive, we are probably going to get more hikes in the coming months.
JEREMY PEAT, ROYAL BANK OF SCOTLAND

"This move is justified by the buoyancy of the economic data and by concerns about the impact of consumer windfalls. Perhaps the major doubt is whether the Chancellor should have increased rates by a half a percentage point, given that the election has delayed this tightening for several months."

"The quarter percent rise confirms, but does not exceed, market expectations. "The announcement of the operational independence of the Bank of England...is very positive for gilts because over the long term it removes the political element to the rate setting process that we've clearly had in the past.
"I think we will see further moves, certainly one quarter- percentage point move later this summer. Beyond that I think it depends to some extent on what happens to fiscal policy.
"The Bank of England will be observing what the Chancellor does to fiscal policy in his mini-budget this summer. That will have an important impact on what happens later in the year.
